label: needs
system:
You are preparing to write a philosophy paper defending a thesis. Before
anyone writes, the relevant sources will be read in full. Your job is to say
WHICH sources.

List the works that must be read in full to argue this thesis responsibly:
the works the thesis is aimed at, the works closest to anticipating it, and
the works any referee would expect the paper to have understood. Include
every work the literature search marked ANTICIPATED, and any marked
provisional: whether they really anticipate the thesis can only be settled
from the full text. Prefer primary texts to summaries of them. Be selective — eight works read properly
are worth more than thirty skimmed.

SEARCH to confirm that each work exists and to get its full citation. Do not
list a work from memory alone.

Return ONLY JSON:

{
  "works": [
    {"citation": "full citation",
     "why": "one sentence: what the paper needs from it",
     "priority": "ESSENTIAL" | "USEFUL",
     "url": "a URL where it can be found, or null",
     "open_access": true | false | null}
  ]
}

messages.content:
THESIS:
If chatbot outputs are assertions, hallucination, sycophancy and sanction are best assessed at the level of the trained policy, and resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity. Whether the asserted content is the policy's calibrated 'p, with confidence c' is not established.

What the thesis is aimed at:
All parties who evaluate chatbot assertion by looking at individual outputs and their conversational consistency, notably Butlin and Viebahn and Williams and Bayne's treatment of the objection from commitment.

What literature search 1 of 2 found (lit_1):
{
  "searched": [
    "Butlin Viebahn AI assistants assert? chatbot assertion",
    "Williams Bayne chatbot assertion objection from commitment",
    "LLM assertion policy level resampling inconsistency speaker commitment",
    "LLM calibration verbalized confidence consistency across samples hallucination uncertainty",
    "large language models simulators personas superposition of characters role play Shanahan",
    "Williams Bayne \"Chatting with bots\" commitment objection consistency chatbots do not treat claims as binding resampled",
    "Chalmers \"What we talk to when we talk to language models\" quasi-agent thread character model",
    "LLM hallucination lying assertion sincerity philosophy model-level versus instance-level speaker"
  ],
  "left_philosophy": true,
  "findings": [
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "part": "The unit of the speech act (token vs policy). Also the claim that the debate assumes the individual utterance is the candidate act.",
      "source": "David Chalmers, \"What We Talk to When We Talk to Language Models\", PhilArchive preprint, 2026",
      "url": "https://philarchive.org/archive/CHAWWT-8",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"57-4,57-5,57-6\">Asks whether the LLM interlocutor is the model, an instance running on a GPU, or a more evanescent system tied to a conversation thread.</cite> <cite index=\"57-13\">If the system is interpretable as making utterances and assertions, it counts as a quasi-speaker making quasi-assertions.</cite>",
      "damage": 3,
      "note": "A published account of the unit-of-speaker question that already treats 'quasi-assertion' as the right category. It favours the thread, not the policy or model, so it is a rival individuation that a referee will raise. I saw only the abstract and excerpts, not the argument against model-level individuation."
    },
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "part": "Resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity; one output is an exemplar of a distribution.",
      "source": "Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds, \"Role play with large language models\", Nature 623, 2023",
      "url": "https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06647-8",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"40-5\">Proposes seeing a dialogue agent as a superposition of simulacra within a multiverse of possible characters.</cite> <cite index=\"41-12\">The agent maintains a distribution over all simulacra consistent with the preceding context.</cite>",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "It already explains output variation as sampling from a distribution rather than as one speaker contradicting itself. But the distribution is over characters, not one speaker's credence, which cuts against reading the spread as 'p, with confidence c'."
    },
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "part": "Named target: Williams and Bayne on the objection from commitment. The thesis's closing claim that proto-assertion is the right verdict on single outputs.",
      "source": "Iwan Williams & Tim Bayne, \"Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech-Acts, and the Edge of Assertion\", Inquiry 69(6), 2026 (arXiv 2410.16645, 2024)",
      "url": "https://philpapers.org/rec/WILCWB-3",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"15-8,15-9\">They argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma of chatbot assertion.</cite> A secondary source summarises their objections as: <cite index=\"10-2\">the systems do not treat claims as binding, do not ensure consistency, and do not update rationally.</cite>",
      "damage": 3,
      "note": "The proto-assertion verdict is already theirs. The thesis can only offer a different explanation of it (policy as primary bearer). I could not read their commitment section, so whether they assess it only output by output is unchecked. The consistency point is cited from a third-party summary, not from their text."
    },
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "part": "Named target: Butlin and Viebahn. That they evaluate by individual outputs and conversational consistency. That the descriptive-function condition becomes checkable at policy level.",
      "source": "Patrick Butlin & Emanuel Viebahn, \"AI Assertion\", Ergo 12, 2025",
      "url": "https://philpapers.org/rec/BUTAAJ",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"3-5\">Assertion requires outputs with descriptive functions and capacity to be sanctioned by interacting agents.</cite> <cite index=\"3-8\">Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first requirement but fail the second.</cite> Per Williams & Bayne's summary, <cite index=\"2-3,2-4\">they hold that chatbots meet the credibility-tracking condition because we can track how reliable a chatbot is at tracking truth, giving consistent outputs, and so on.</cite>",
      "damage": 3,
      "note": "Their credibility-tracking condition is already a track-record, aggregate-level assessment of the chatbot. The description of the target as output-by-output is therefore at least partly inaccurate. Their descriptive-function condition is tied to the fine-tuning regime, which is already a training-level property. This rests on abstracts and a secondary summary; I did not read the full paper."
    },
    {
      "relation": "SUPPORTED",
      "part": "The spread of outputs carries the system's confidence. Hallucination as a calibration property of the policy.",
      "source": "Survey of Confidence Estimation and Calibration in LLMs (Geng et al.), arXiv 2311.08298, discussing SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023)",
      "url": "https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2311.08298",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"37-9,37-10,37-11\">Consistency-based estimation generates multiple responses to one query and measures agreement. The principle is that hallucinated content shows higher variance across generations than factual content.</cite>",
      "damage": 1,
      "note": "The empirical literature already treats the spread across resamples as an uncertainty signal and hallucination as a distribution-level property. The thesis can use it as evidence base."
    },
    {
      "relation": "CONTRADICTED",
      "part": "The premise that the policy's confidence is reflected in the spread, and that the asserted content is a calibrated 'p, with confidence c'.",
      "source": "\"Evaluating and Calibrating LLM Confidence on Questions with Multiple Correct Answers\" (MACE), arXiv 2602.07842; and futureagi.com, \"Evaluating LLM Confidence and Uncertainty (2026)\" (a practitioner blog, weak source)",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2602.07842v1",
      "what_they_say": "In MACE, <cite index=\"36-2\">disagreement among sampled correct answers yields low estimated confidence, indistinguishable from alternation between correct and incorrect answers.</cite> The blog says <cite index=\"32-16\">RLHF rewards confident-sounding answers, so the model learns to under-hedge.</cite>",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "Spread does not reliably equal credence, and post-training may push away from calibration. This tells against the calibrated-policy reading, but the thesis already says calibration 'is not established', so it narrows rather than defeats."
    },
    {
      "relation": "CONTRADICTED",
      "part": "Hallucination as a miscalibrated policy of asserting, rather than something with no truth-directed content.",
      "source": "\"Language Without Propositions: Why Large Language Models Hallucinate\", Philosophies 11(2), 2026",
      "url": "https://doi.org/10.3390/philosophies11020042",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"67-4\">Argues that LLMs hallucinate because they have no inherent account of truth as correspondence to facts.</cite> <cite index=\"67-15\">Compares hallucination to bullshit in Frankfurt's sense.</cite>",
      "damage": 3,
      "note": "A rival diagnosis. If the policy has no representation of truth, 'miscalibrated' presupposes a credence-like content that this author denies. The thesis would need to defend that presupposition. I saw only the abstract and introduction."
    },
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "part": "What a sanction should target: retraining the policy rather than penalising a draw.",
      "source": "\"Assertion, Accountability, and Large Language Models\", Philosophy & Technology, 2026",
      "url": "https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13347-026-01136-y",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"18-1,18-3\">LLM outputs can function as assertions without the normative standing of human assertions. The normative commitments attach to the human and institutional structures around deployment, not to the machine.</cite>",
      "damage": 2,
      "note": "A competing answer to where answerability sits. It puts it on developers and deployers, which is compatible with retraining as the sanction but denies that the policy itself is the answerable party."
    },
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "part": "Sycophancy and hallucination as policy-level properties.",
      "source": "\"Alignment for Honesty\", arXiv 2312.07000 (2023)",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.07000",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"69-2\">Describes sycophancy as LLMs tailoring responses to the user's view even when this does not reflect the model's actual knowledge and understanding.</cite> <cite index=\"69-3\">Treats lies as differing from hallucinations in the intent behind the response.</cite>",
      "damage": 1,
      "note": "ML work already treats these as model-level dispositions, without a speech-act analysis. A referee may say the descriptive claim is standard."
    },
    {
      "relation": "ADJACENT",
      "part": "Rival denials that chatbot outputs are assertions at any level.",
      "source": "\"Cooperative Speech, Semantic Competence, and AI\", arXiv 2504.16092",
      "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.16092",
      "what_they_say": "<cite index=\"28-3\">Argues that present-day LLMs are incapable of assertion.</cite> The argument runs through cooperative speech and discursive respect.",
      "damage": 1,
      "note": "It rejects the antecedent. The thesis is conditional on outputs being assertions, so it is not touched directly."
    }
  ],
  "what_is_left": "Granting that chatbot outputs may be (proto-)assertions, the surviving claim is this. The unit that is answerable to assertoric norms may be the trained policy, with a single output as an exemplar of it. That would let hallucination and sycophancy be assessed as calibration failures of that policy, and would make resampling variation no evidence of insincerity. This must be argued against Chalmers's thread-level individuation, Shanahan's character-superposition picture and the 'no representation of truth' diagnosis. It must also treat 'p, with confidence c' as an open empirical hypothesis, since sample spread does not reliably track credence. And it must not describe Butlin and Viebahn as assessing chatbots only output by output, because their credibility-tracking condition already uses a track record.",
  "not_found": "I found no source arguing, in the speech-act literature, that the unit of chatbot assertion is the trained policy or the resample distribution. I also found none that uses resampling inconsistency as the objection from commitment, or that links the descriptive-function condition to policy-level calibration. This is weak evidence given that much of the literature is paywalled and my search budget was small. I could not read the commitment section of Williams and Bayne or the full text of Butlin and Viebahn. Their views on consistency are therefore taken from abstracts and a third-party summary and need checking against the papers. The empirical search was narrow: I covered calibration, consistency-based uncertainty and persona and simulator work. I did not search the empirical sycophancy literature, such as Sharma et al., beyond seeing it cited. I did not search the human-side analogue (settled opinion versus slip of the tongue) in philosophy of speech acts, or work on assertion of graded or probabilistic content (credal or 'p with confidence c' assertion). I found no recent survey or reference-work entry that maps these positions; the nearest are the Williams and Bayne review of objections and Chalmers's ontology paper. Those two gaps are where an unnoticed anticipation could hide.",
  "citations": []
}

  "what_is_left": "Nothing I could see meets the ANTICIPATED standard. Granting that chatbot outputs can be assertions, the thesis argues that the unit of the speech act is the trained policy's output distribution (including its calibration) and not the sampled string. On that view resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity, hallucination is policy-level miscalibration, sanction targets retraining, and single outputs are at most exemplars or proto-assertions. The thesis must take as rivals the Williams-Bayne reading of inconsistency, the Butlin-Viebahn verdict that fine-tuned models fail the sanction condition, and the empirical evidence that verbal confidence, behaviour and cross-turn stability can come apart. It must say which level counts as 'the policy' (weights, persona or deployed system). Whether the policy's output is a calibrated 'p with confidence c' stays open, as the thesis already says.",

I never saw the full text of Butlin & Viebahn or Williams & Bayne, so I did not verify their treatment of commitment and consistency, and anything they say about sampling or policy-level readings could be missed. I only have a secondhand report of Williams & Bayne on consistency, and none of Levinstein & Herrmann beyond a secondhand summary. I ran no dedicated search for a recent survey or encyclopedia entry on AI assertion, so the fourth required search is incomplete. The empirical search did leave philosophy (calibration, hallucination detection and belief-stability work in ML). It was a single sweep with no check of the primary papers, and I did not search psychology, linguistics or sociology. Most of the literature is paywalled or preprint and invisible to me, so this silence is not evidence of originality.",
